q: Why do agile teams prefer counting finished features over reporting "percent done"?
options: Finished features are easier to estimate in hours
Finished features are empirical data, while percent done is a prediction that often proves wrong
Percent done is forbidden by the Agile Manifesto
Finished features do not need to be tested
explanation: Surrogate measures such as percent done depend on the team's ability to predict completion. Finished, working features are empirical and show the true state of the project.

q: A project is reported green every month, then turns red one month before release. What is this called?
options: A spike
Gold plating
Uncontrolled scope creep
A watermelon project
explanation: A watermelon project is green on the outside and red on the inside: the status looks fine because there is no empirical data until late in the project.

q: A team wants a chart that shows, day by day, whether the work left in the sprint will fit the time left. What does a burndown chart plot?
options: Work remaining versus the time left in a timebox
Work completed so far, measured against total scope
The number of defects found per release
The cost variance of each iteration
explanation: A burndown chart is a graphical representation of the work remaining versus the time left in a timebox.

q: A product owner added several stories during a release. Which chart makes that added scope easiest to see?
options: Iteration burndown chart
Gantt chart
Burnup chart
Cause-and-effect diagram
explanation: A burnup chart draws the total work as a line across the top and the completed work rising from zero. When scope is added, the top line moves up, so the change is visible.

q: Halfway through an iteration, the actual line on the burndown chart is above the ideal line. What does this mean?
options: The team is ahead of plan
More work remains than planned, so the team is behind
Scope has been removed
The chart has been drawn incorrectly and should be redone
explanation: The burndown chart plots work remaining. An actual line above the ideal line means more work remains than planned at that point, so the team is behind.

q: A team completed 18, 22 and 20 story points in its last three iterations. 100 points remain. About how many iterations are left?
explanation: Average velocity = (18 + 22 + 20) ÷ 3 = 20 points per iteration. 100 ÷ 20 = 5 iterations.

q: A director wants to rank three teams by their velocity. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because velocity is an objective measure of productivity
Agree, but only after converting story points to hours
Ask each team to raise its velocity by 10% first
Explain that velocity is specific to each team and should not be used to compare or judge teams
explanation: Velocity is a lightweight, team-specific planning aid. Story points differ between teams, and using velocity to compare or rank people creates fear and a loss of transparency.

q: What tends to happen when velocity becomes a target set by management?
options: Estimates become more accurate
The team needs fewer retrospectives
Teams inflate estimates, split work unnaturally or sacrifice quality
Lead time always falls
explanation: Making velocity a target creates perverse incentives: teams may inflate estimates, split work unnaturally or cut quality to meet the number.

q: A customer requests a feature on day 1. The team starts work on day 11 and delivers on day 15. What is the lead time?
options: 14 days
4 days
10 days
11 days
explanation: Lead time runs from the customer's request to delivery: day 1 to day 15 is 14 days. The 4 days from start of work to delivery is the cycle time.

q: A team starts work on a feature on 11 March and finishes it on 15 March. Which metric measures this elapsed time, from when work on an item starts to when it is finished?
options: Lead time
Throughput
Velocity
Total cycle time
explanation: Cycle time is the total elapsed time from the start of a work item to its completion. Lead time starts earlier, at the request.

q: A Kanban team reports a throughput of 14 last week and 15 the week before. What is throughput?
options: The number of items waiting in a queue
The number of work items finished per time period
The total story points still remaining in the backlog
The time an item spends waiting
explanation: Throughput is the count of work items finished per time period. Stable throughput lets a team forecast and spot sudden drops in productivity.

q: On a cumulative flow diagram, the "in test" band grows wider every week. What does this indicate?
options: Testing is ahead of development
Throughput is increasing
A bottleneck: work is entering testing faster than it leaves
The team's velocity has stabilized after several iterations of work
explanation: A band that keeps widening shows items accumulating in that state. Growing queues signal bottlenecks and hidden delays.

q: After each release, customers report defects that the team then has to fix, and the amount is growing. Which metric is a direct indicator of product quality and of whether the team's pace is sustainable?
options: Queue length in each state
Throughput
Lead time
Escaped defects and rework
explanation: Escaped defects are issues found after release. Together with the effort spent fixing them, they indicate product quality and the sustainability of the pace.

q: Which of these is an outcome measure rather than a flow measure?
options: Customer satisfaction or Net Promoter Score
Cycle time
Work in process at the end of each iteration
Queue length
explanation: Flow metrics show how efficiently the team delivers. Outcome measures such as customer satisfaction, business value delivered and adoption show what was delivered and its effect.

q: A team keeps a large board on the wall beside its desks, showing the stories in progress and the burndown chart, and updates it by hand each day. Which statement about this information radiator is correct?
options: It is a confidential report sent to the sponsor
It is updated once, at the end of the project
It is a visible display, easy to update, placed where people can readily see it
It must be produced by scheduling software
explanation: An information radiator is a visible, physical display that shares information with the rest of the organization. It is posted where people can see it, is easy to update and is updated often.

q: A column on the team's board is close to its work-in-progress limit. What should team members do?
options: Raise the limit so more work can start
Swarm: help finish the work in that column before starting new work
Move the items back to the backlog
Wait for the next retrospective
explanation: When a column approaches its work-in-progress limit, team members can swarm around the current work to help those working on the tasks that are slowing the flow.

q: A sponsor asks when the remaining 45 stories will be finished. What is the best way to answer?
options: Give a range with a confidence level, based on the team's throughput
Give a single fixed date now and commit the whole team to meeting it
Say that agile teams do not forecast
Give the date in the original plan
explanation: Combining stable throughput with an up-to-date item count allows probabilistic forecasts. Forecasts should be presented as ranges or confidence levels, never as single-point commitments.

q: At the end of an iteration the team meets, without stakeholders, to look at how it worked. What is this retrospective for?
options: To show working product to stakeholders
To decide which stories will go into the next iteration backlog
To identify who caused the iteration's problems
To let the team learn from its work and improve its process
explanation: The retrospective allows the team to learn about, improve and adapt its process. It is not about blame.

q: A retrospective produces twelve improvement ideas. What should the team do?
options: Commit to all twelve in the next iteration
Pass the list to the product owner to decide
Rank them and take on only as many as it has capacity to complete
Record all twelve and review them together at the end of the project
explanation: The team ranks the improvement items and limits them to its capacity. Trying to improve too many things and finishing none is much worse than completing a few.

q: A flow-based team does not use iterations. When should it hold a retrospective?
options: Never, because a retrospective only makes sense at the end of an iteration
After a release, when a few weeks have passed, or when work is stuck
Only at the end of the project
Only when the sponsor asks for one
explanation: A team does not need iterations to retrospect. It may do so when it ships something, when more than a few weeks have passed, when work is not flowing, or at any other milestone.

q: A stakeholder asks to join the team's retrospective, because she attended last week's demonstration and found it useful. How does a retrospective differ from a demonstration (review)?
options: The retrospective is attended by customers; the demonstration is not
The retrospective happens before the iteration starts; the demonstration happens after
There is no difference
The retrospective examines how the team works; the demonstration examines the product
explanation: A demonstration presents completed product to stakeholders for feedback. A retrospective is the team exploring its work and results to improve its process.

q: What must be true of the setting for a retrospective to work?
options: It is psychologically safe, so members can speak candidly without fear of blame
Senior management attends to approve the actions
Only quantitative data is discussed
It is skipped when the iteration went well
explanation: A retrospective needs a psychologically safe space where every member can speak candidly and share feedback without fear of blame or retaliation. It uses both qualitative and quantitative data.

q: An agile team planned to complete 40 story points in an iteration and completed 30. Using the 2017 Agile Practice Guide's way of expressing earned value in agile terms, what is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
explanation: In agile terms SPI = completed features (or points) ÷ planned features. 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75: the team is working at 75% of the rate planned.

q: A team has spent $200,000 so far and has completed features worth $150,000 of the planned value. What is its cost performance index (CPI), and what does it mean?
options: 1.33: the project is under budget
0.75: 75 cents of value for each dollar spent
0.75: the team is three quarters of the way to done
1.33: the team is ahead of schedule
explanation: CPI = earned value ÷ actual cost = 150,000 ÷ 200,000 = 0.75. The project is getting 75 cents of value for each dollar spent. In agile, earned value is based on finished features.

q: A card is added to a team's board on Monday. Nobody starts work on it until Thursday. In the 2017 Agile Practice Guide, what is the time between Monday and Thursday called?
options: Response time
Cycle time
Lead time
Velocity
explanation: Response time is the time an item waits until work starts. Cycle time is the time required to process the item, and lead time is the total from when it is added to the board until it is completed.

q: On a feature chart, the "features complete" line rises steadily, but the "total features" line has stepped up three times since the start. What does the chart show?
options: The team is finishing work more slowly each month
The team has stopped delivering features
Requirements grew during the project
The budget was increased three times
explanation: A feature burnup/burndown chart shows features complete, features remaining and total features. A total line that rises shows that requirements grew during the project.

q: A team reports that it "earned" 45 story points this iteration, but most of those points belong to stories that are started and not finished. According to the 2017 Agile Practice Guide, what is wrong?
options: Story points may be reported only by the product owner
The team should have reported hours, not points
Nothing: points for started work are valid progress
It measures capacity, not finished work
explanation: Measuring story points is not the same as measuring completed stories or features. A team that measures only story points measures capacity, not finished work, which violates the principle that a working product is the primary measure of progress.
